title: Garage Floor Epoxy & Polyaspartic Coating | Florida
description: Garage floor epoxy and polyaspartic coating systems for North Central Florida: diamond-ground slabs, moisture testing, flake broadcast, UV-stable topcoat.
h1: Garage Floor Epoxy Coating Systems Built for Florida Slabs
heroIntro: Diamond grinding, moisture testing, an epoxy basecoat, full flake broadcast, and a polyaspartic topcoat that resists hot tires, chemicals, and Florida sun.
card: Ground, moisture-tested slabs coated with epoxy, flake, and a UV-stable polyaspartic topcoat that resists hot tires.

sections.h2: What a real garage floor coating system includes
body: "Epoxy floor" covers everything from a one-coat kit rolled over an acid-washed slab to a multi-layer system on ground concrete. They look similar for a month. After a summer of hot tires, they do not. A garage floor epoxy coating worth paying for is a system, and each layer has a job:
bullets: Mechanical prep by diamond grinding to open the concrete surface
Crack, spall, and control joint repair
A penetrating epoxy basecoat, or a moisture-mitigating primer where testing calls for it
Full or partial decorative flake broadcast for texture and slip resistance
A UV-stable polyaspartic topcoat that resists abrasion, chemicals, and yellowing

body: Power-troweled garage slabs have a dense, slick surface layer. Acid etching and big-box kits barely scratch it, so the coating sits on top instead of locking in. The first time a car parks on a 90-degree afternoon, softened tires grab the coating and pull it up in patches, a failure called hot tire pickup.

Diamond grinding removes that top layer and leaves a defined profile the epoxy can soak into. Dust is captured by a vacuum during grinding. If you are dealing with a floor that has already let go, our article on why garage epoxy peels and how to fix it covers what removal and recoating involve.

Our water table and humidity push vapor up through slabs that lack an effective vapor barrier underneath. Epoxy over a wet slab can blister and delaminate no matter how well it was ground. Before the system is chosen, the crew lead checks moisture. A normal reading means a standard epoxy basecoat. Elevated readings mean a moisture-mitigating primer first, and on rare slabs the honest advice is not to coat at all.

sections.h2: Epoxy vs. polyaspartic: how the layers work together
body: Epoxy is the workhorse basecoat. It penetrates ground concrete well, builds thickness, and holds flake firmly. Its weakness is UV: exposed to sunlight from an open garage door, plain epoxy yellows and chalks. Polyaspartic is a fast-curing coating that stays clear and color-stable in sunlight and resists scratches and chemicals better, but it is less forgiving as a primer.

Combining them gives you the best of both: epoxy bonding to the slab, polyaspartic protecting the surface. Flake broadcast adds texture so the floor is less slick when wet, and it hides minor imperfections and dust between cleanings. Solid-color finishes without flake are available for workshops and showrooms that want a cleaner look, sometimes with an added grit for traction.

sections.h2: Choosing colors, flake blends, and finish options
body: Most homeowners pick a full flake broadcast in a blended color such as gray, tan, or a mixed granite look. Full broadcast means the basecoat is covered completely with flake, which gives the most texture and hides tire marks and dust well. Partial broadcast scatters flake over a solid color for a cleaner, more modern look, but it shows dirt a little more readily. Solid color with no flake suits workshops where small parts get dropped and need to be found.

Edges matter too. The coating is usually carried a few inches up the stem wall to create a cove that is easy to clean, and the transition at the garage door is finished neatly so water from the driveway does not get under the coating. Control joints can be filled and coated over, or left open and honored so the floor's natural movement does not crack the finish. We will walk through these choices with you and note them on the estimate.
If you store a boat, use a home gym, or keep a second fridge in the garage, mention it on the walkthrough. Heavy point loads and rubber mats affect which topcoat and thickness make sense.

A coated floor wipes clean of oil, brake fluid, and lawn clippings, and it brightens the garage by reflecting light. Routine care is sweeping and an occasional mop with a mild cleaner. Avoid dragging heavy steel equipment without pads. Chips from dropped tools can be spot repaired, and the polyaspartic topcoat can be recoated down the road without grinding back to bare concrete.

For the hiring side of the decision, including what install day looks like and how long until you can drive on it, see our page on hiring local epoxy garage floor installers. Coatings for walls, block, and other concrete surfaces are covered under concrete and masonry painting, and all of our floor and coating work is listed with our specialty services.

faqs.q: What is better, epoxy or polyaspartic?
faqs.a: For most garages the best answer is both: an epoxy basecoat for bonding and build, and a polyaspartic topcoat for UV stability and abrasion resistance.

faqs.q: Why did my DIY epoxy kit peel?
faqs.a: Usually because acid etching did not open the slab enough for the coating to bond, so hot tires pulled it loose. Diamond grinding solves that.
Yes. Slab moisture determines whether a standard basecoat will hold or a moisture-mitigating primer is needed, and occasionally whether the slab should be coated at all.

faqs.q: Does flake make the floor slippery?
faqs.a: Flake adds texture, so a broadcast floor is generally less slick than a smooth solid coat. Extra anti-slip additive can be added to the topcoat if needed.
